newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Milburn's China investment problematic.
newsitem.headline: Milburn's China investment problematic.

text.p: Cement producer Milburn New Zealand Ltd said on Monday its two-year-old investment in China was proving tougher than expected but it planned to stay for the long term.

Earlier, the company reported a 6.6 percent rise in net profit in 1996 to NZ$24.3 milllion. Its operating profit rose 15.7 percent to $49.9 million excluding its investment in the Golden Cat Cement Works in Suzhou, 100 km from Shanghai.

Milburn jointly owns a 50.1 percent stake in Golden Cat with two Singaporean partners. Milburn itself is 73 percent owned by giant Swiss building materials group Holderbank Fianciere Glaris Ltd, the world's largest cement producer.
Milburn's equity accounted losses in China in 1996 were NZ$4.9 million compared with $2.5 million a year earlier when it predicted its China operations were heading for profit.
Managing Director Bill Townsend said a lift in cement prices in China to more realistic levels was not expected for some time as China kept credit conditions tight in an effort to fight inflation.
A relaxation of government monetary controls as inflation was brought under control should assist Golden Cat but not for some time, Townsend said.
"We didn't foresee the economy slowing down. We entered into China in early 1995 and...we thought things would continue as they had for the previous few years," he told Reuters.
"We didn't see that slowdown or the tight money supply coming up," he said.

Tight credit controls weakened cement demand and severe price competition in the oversupplied Shanghai market, and liquidity problems among construction companies depressed sales revenue, trading results and debtor collections for Golden Cat.

Many projects had been slowed down or deferred and of those continuing, "triangular debt" had developed where a building owner was short of cash and failed to pay contractors who in turn failed to pay the suppliers.

"There is not enough cash for the amount of development going on. That has created a market where people are reluctant to sell products for any other basis than cash on delivery because the chances are that you may not get paid unless they are very large, reliable organisations."
The situation had not deteriorated since the death of Chinese paramount leader Deng Xiaoping last month.

Interest rates had eased in the last 6-8 months but money supply had not been loosened. Townsend said that the indications were that supply would be eased gradually but the construction sector as a lagging indicator would be slow to recover.
"I would think it would be late in this year at the earliest before we see some relief in the low (cement) pricing."
Townsend said Milburn was not reviewing its investment.
"It hasn't performed to our expectations so far but we are in it for the long-term."
Prospects for cement production in New Zealand were seen as continuing to improve, as they had since a trough in 1992.
"We still see that there will be a slight increase this year and prospects for the longer-term look pretty good," he said.
Townsend saw a pickup in commercial industrial and residential building, and increased government spending would be directed towards the infrastructure area.
"We see it as a reasonably good outlook for the New Zealand construction economy," Townsend said.
Milburn's share price fell five cents to to $3.00. Analysts generally viewed the result as positive in a general environment of falling profits.

But one, who declined to be identified, said that Milburn had joined a growing list of New Zealand companies, including brewer Lion Nathan and Fletcher Challenge Building, losing money in China with poor future prospects.
-- Wellington newsroom 64 4 4734 746
